It would be hard for human civilisation to develop on a tidally locked planet for sure. But who's to say another civilisation would have a problem with this? There are lifeforms on earth that can and do sense infrared light, they don't need the sun to provide this. There's also plenty of life that lives in the deep ocean where there isn't any light.
And how many of these lifeforms have developed sophisticated technologies that would indicate civilization?

How many lifeforms on earth have developed sophisticated technologies as well? One. A single lifeform has developed civilisation. It's exceedingly rare, but just because this world was suited to this type of lifeform, another world may be suited to a different lifeform.

The other thing is we don't actually know much about what's at the bottom of the ocean. I'm highly skeptical that there is any advanced life down there, but that doesn't make it impossible. Advanced life of all types is unlikely. It took humans thousands of years to get where they are today.

I'm not disagreeing with this. Anything is possible. But we're talking about whether it's more likely for technologically advanced life forms to develop on earth-like planets, or "extreme" planets with conditions not favorable to life and "civilization" as we know it. Based on everything we know, earth-like planets would be more favorable (winds below, eg, 800mph, temperatures right around a state (solid liquid gas) boundary for soluble material, eg, water).

And it actually took humans a few million years to get where we are, based on what we know today, but regardless, that's still a drop in the bucket geologically, or universally.

You have to remember, that evolution is essentially the development of life that suits the circumstances because the suitable life dies out. It's possible that humans can evolve on a tidally locked planet but with more suitable adaptations that will allow them to build civilisation like we did on earth. Anyway it's impossible to know.
